pitch_detail.notes: Several ways reach the ledgy pod below the splitter; the right-hand option starts from the small spruce at the base. Low-angle ledgy slab leads to a big grassy ledge. Skip the tempting leftward traverse into the corner and climb straight up through a few strenuous moves to hidden jugs on the face, then right through blocky ground to just under an obvious overhang. A steep tight crack with finger pods guards the final traverse, which is the hardest part of the pitch: sequential moves on tricky hands, then left along thin footholds to a jug and into the pod, where the anchor is. A 70 m rope would reach the ground from here, but lowering is not recommended.

The crux of the route. Start from the pod with a thin vertical finger crack that becomes a tight right-facing dihedral; the first moves off the belay are insecure finger jams and liebacks on small feet. Holds on the right-hand face ease the dihedral. A small roof at its top has excellent hand jams to pull onto the face above, then face climbing with crack protection leads to a triangular pod. A large pegmatite boulder in the conglomerate to the right is the next obvious anchor if you split the lead. Pitches 2 and 3 can be linked into about 150 ft of continuous crack.

Follow the splitter crack above the triangular pod up to a flat ledge. Plenty of face holds, finger locks and the odd sinker pocket make it steady climbing on unusual rock. The last 20 ft steepen and the crack narrows to tight fingers before the ledge.
From the ledge, climb an awkward short chimney, then scramble right to the summit block.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches with grades and lengths converted from feet. Crux marked on P2 (named as route crux). No rappel table: descent is a walk-off and the only rappel mention is a P1 aside.
review.other_findings: Stored grade 5.10 and 4 pitches agree. Descent walks off north via low 5th-class moves to a saddle, not a rappel.

pitch_detail.notes: Two starts exist. The direct start is much harder, rarely in, runout, around WI4 M5. The more reasonable start, to the climber's right, is still somewhat runout: pull an awkward but well-protected bulge, then follow a mixed runnel to the big ledge below the main flow.
Take the left-hand portion of the principal ice flow, stopping under the large overhang.
Traverse left to avoid the steep overhanging ice dagger, then pick a line up blocky terrain to the low-angle terrace. This can be linked with the pitch below.
Continue up the gully, if it has ice, for one or two more pitches.

review.changed: Wrote P1-P3 and combined P4-5 entry as described. No anchors or lengths stated, so none written. No rappel table: descent is a scramble west or an unspecified rap.
review.other_findings: Stored 5 pitches; P4-5 entry covers one or two pitches. Stored WI4+ M4-5: direct P1 start is WI4 M5 R/X, normal P1 WI4- M4.

pitch_detail.notes: Same start as the neighbouring flow. Choose the right-hand runnel (M4) or the clear line of weakness just left of it (M1). Belay at a boulder on the terrace with one bolt plus some gear.
Climb the main flow for about 30 ft, then traverse right, move onto the rock, heading for a V-shaped groove that gains the ledge. Building a belay is difficult here.
Traverse along the ledge, past a thin smear of ice and a fixed rappel anchor, to a belay in a protected alcove before the next pitch.
The obvious golden corner: steep and well protected. Belay in the WI3 bulge.

Follow the ice runnel that angles left, pass left of the rotten yellow overhang and continue on easy, well-protected ground to low-angle third-class terrain. A rappel anchor sits at the top of this pitch.
Work left and join the upper section of the neighbouring route. It may be quicker to walk west down scree and talus instead.

rappel_detail.anchor: fixed rappel anchor at top of pitch 5
rappel_detail.notes: Reaches the other fixed rappel anchor on the ledge.

rappel_detail.anchor: fixed rappel anchor on the ledge
rappel_detail.notes: Rappel directly down from the ledge to the bolted anchor of a summer sport climb.

rappel_detail.anchor: 2 bolts on a summer sport route
rappel_detail.notes: Two bolts; this rappel reaches the ground.

review.changed: Wrote 6 pitches and a 3-station rappel table. Pitch 1 grade shows both stated options. Station 2 length not stated.
review.other_findings: Stored grade WI4 M5 PG13 vs. pitch grades topping at M4; no M5 stated here.

pitch_detail.notes: First 150 ft of ice with some mixed moves, ending at a belay that is also the rappel point for descent.
Second 150 ft pitch, easier on the mixed side. From the top, walk off down to the first belay.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches, lengths converted from 150 ft. No rappel table: only a single rappel from the first belay is mentioned.

pitch_detail.notes: Broken corners around a flake lead to a bushy alcove belay. Small pieces build the anchor; save hand-size cams for the next pitch.
The arching crack: hand, fist and finger sizes, jammed and laybacked to a ledge. A couple of old fixed anchors on the ledge are rusty and best not trusted.

A short easy section to a belay in the gully, roughly 50 ft though the length is uncertain. Beyond that, a 5.5 gully can be simul-climbed, or the final 200 ft soloed; bear right once past the slot, with plenty of easy variations.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches. P3 length is hedged so left out of lengthM. Crux set on P2 (route's top grade).

pitch_detail.notes: Usually climbed on rock to a hanging dagger of ice past a fixed pin. With less ice, a hand-crack ramp to the left works, or you can skip the pitch by walking in along a ledge coming from the right.
Follow an ice or mixed groove, shallow and facing right, up to the foot of the headwall; thin ice may be detached from the rock, so test it. Climb over the pillar and continue on gentler ice.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches without grades (none stated per pitch).
review.other_findings: None; conditions vary from mixed to ice to the ground.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin at the west end of the feature, beside a large gully, where a clean seamed corner has a small bulge roughly 20 ft up. Pass the bulge and keep following the corner system on fair rock until a ledge at 60 m, where you belay.
Work up and right across the ledge system to the foot of a second corner. Hollow-sounding rock here. Pick your belay with care: it is directly in the line of anything the next leader dislodges.
Follow the corner system until it becomes hiking terrain. Many loose blocks.
Hike about 100 m to the ridge and reach the top of the pinnacle from its north side.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches; P4 is hiking. Crux set on P1 as route's top grade. No rappels.
review.other_findings: Stored 3 pitches; description has a 4th class 100 m section. Gear is sparse; smaller sizes mostly.

pitch_detail.notes: The pitch begins in the gap separating the red pillar from the west ridge. A 5.9 crack leads to a stance, then an easy but loose slab with real runout to a belay. The crack section is fairly solid; the rock above is loose.
Follow broken cracks to a roof, pass it on the left, then take a corner to a large ledge.
Hike through scree to a prominent gully on the left, then climb it past a 5.6 chimney to a great ledge.
A splitter layback. Soloing separates this from the earlier pitches.
Three cracks cut the headwall. A 5.4 gully or slot is easy enough to solo; a harder offwidth or an eroding hand crack are the alternatives.
Headwall hand crack, a standout pitch.
Wind up a ramp to a final bulge, finishing on the summit plateau, from which a short hike reaches the top.

review.changed: Wrote 7 pitches. No crux set (two 5.9 pitches). Lengths and anchors not stated. No rappels.
review.other_findings: Stored grade 5.9 R agrees; much soloing between roped pitches; rock quality variable.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb high on stemmy 5.7 features on grainy rock before the first protection. Then two or three pieces are available out left; climb up and right toward an offwidth that takes a #1 and finish on a good ledge.
The chossy corner up and right has good cracks and plenty of gear. Top out and belay from gear.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches without grades; a 5.7 stemming section is described in P1 notes.
review.other_findings: Stored length 30 m is short for two pitches and grade 5.8+ PG13 not repeated in text.

pitch_detail.notes: The central crack of the buttress gives varied, pleasant climbing. A slung horn makes the belay.
Climb the slot above, favouring the sound rock on its right, then easier ground carries on to the buttress top.
Shift the belay up and right, following a grassy earth spine to the foot of an alcove.
Leave the alcove up and to the left on decent rock. Anchor with a horn and a cam.
Climb a grass gully for about 5 m, then right onto rock spines and over onto a slab. A blunt arete up and right is the next objective; anchor at its base.
Follow the arete up, ending at a loose ledge beside a knife-edge arete on its right.
Climb the knife-edge arete onto easier-angled terrain, then steep grass and a shallow rock slot reach grassy ledges that look across to the upper headwall.
Move the belay up the grassy ledges to just right of the gully that separates the two summits.
Work up the slabs, angling right, to a steep corner.
Climb the steep right-facing corner, watching for loose rock. Pull over the lip onto third-class ground and run out the rope to a belay.
Easier ground leads right to the ridge. When the wall gets steeper, cross over the ridge and belay in a corner under the last hard section.
The final crux: steep cracks through a small bulge on rock that needs testing.
Rambling terrain up and right to a right-facing corner, up it to slabs, then belay.
Continue to the ridge and round to the other side for moderate ledges and grass. The rope can come off here; the summit is second-class hiking.

review.changed: Wrote all 14 pitches with stated grades and lengths. Crux on P12 (named final crux). No rappels: walk-off descent.
review.other_findings: Stored length 305 m vs. about 460 m summed from stated pitch lengths. Grade 5.7+ R matches P12.

pitch_detail.notes: The left fork of the big dihedral at the back of the cirque. Climbing begins near M2-3 and finishes in a heel-and-toe squeeze chimney at M4; it uses the full 60 m of rope.
Mostly snow with the occasional small headwall, heading toward the dark chimney you can see from the base; roughly M1-2.
Further snow and short rock steps to the foot of the dark chimney; roughly M1-2.
Hard work chimneying, with small gear and hook placements on the left wall.
Begins at the foot of the next obvious dark, slightly overhanging squeeze chimney. A little ice was present but not enough for screws. May be combined with the previous pitch.
Easy mixed ground to scrambling up a short gully. Beyond it the descent couloir to Sky Pond is obvious; head north.

review.changed: Wrote 6 pitches. P2 and P3 grades are a hedged range and left in notes; P6 grade is approximate. No fixed gear, no rappels.
review.other_findings: Stored M4-5 vs. text top M4+. No length stored; P1 is 60 m.

pitch_detail.notes: Take the vertical splitter around 50 ft left of the massive dihedral (several variations exist). Near 30 m, jugs lead left to a ledge holding a little corner; continue to the next ledge to the left and set up the belay on its sloping surface. Useful gear: 00, 0.1, 0.2 and a key #2.

Meander up and right, getting past the overhangs on their right through a small corner, then on up good-quality face with no protection. The original line cuts right to a rock scar with loose flakes, then trends up and left beside a huge detached flake to a good ledge. A 5.10- R option heads straight up, left of a corner and roof, on very sparse gear, arriving at that same ledge.

Head straight up through a 5.10+ section of cracks, left to a small ledge, then up and right to the massive left-facing corner, where you can belay if wanted. The 5.11- corner leads to a ledge on the right.
Up and right through an easy wide crack (#4), then take the weakness up as the crack dogs right and go straight up. Mediocre rock, ending at a sloping ledge with a good hand-size crack.
Go left along the sloping ledge to the evident weakness, which runs directly to the top.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches. Crux on P3 (top grade). No rappel table; descent is a 4th-class scramble.

pitch_detail.notes: A small, shallow corner starts the route; quickly move right on jugs to a crack that reaches a ledge. Aim for the ledge's right end and an evident corner, which shifts right then arcs left into another crack, finishing on a narrow foot ledge.

Climb the right-slanting crack, then directly to a roof. Pass it slightly leftward via an overhanging finger-to-hand crack, then thin finger cracks lead up and right. A mantel gains a small ledge at the foot of the big orange pillar; continue up and left past a bush growing in the crack onto a juggy face with two bolts, reaching a ledge and then a stepped ledge with a two-bolt anchor. The 5.11+ PG13 variation climbs the pillar's arete/corner directly, with marginal gear and a fixed piton, until reaching the first bolt on the juggy face.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches. No crux set. No rappel table: bolted anchors exist but stations are not listed; two ropes needed.

pitch_detail.notes: Starting on the neighbouring route is the recommended way. The original start is on a pedestal 100 ft right of that route, below the large roof: climb up and well to the left toward a big orange corner and belay at its foot, where a decayed bail anchor with the remains of a fixed rope can be found.

The poor-quality orange corner leads until you can move right into a crack in better stone, then up to a ledge under the big overhanging roof. A hand-and-finger crack in the left wall brings you onto a slab. From there downclimb left toward the bushy corner, or preferably climb up and left across 5.9 PG13 face above the bushes. That corner finishes at a two-bolt anchor on top of the pillar.
Up and right to the ledge, then right to a left-leaning gully/chimney directly under the big roof crack; up it to a belay ledge on the right.

The left-facing corner has questionable rock; a bulge with a bolt comes next, then the #4-sized crack through a small roof, ending beneath the big roof. Belay here, or shift left to a crack that offers a better stance.

A 40 ft horizontal crack, mainly hand and fist sizes. One bolt protects the bulge of pale rock that gives access to the crack; follow it out the roof to an anchor on the wall where it becomes vertical. Try to keep the second's rope out of the crack, where it could get trapped behind cams.

The splitter continues in the corner, with face holds helping as it grows to #6 size. Just short of where it becomes a rotten chimney, leave it leftward toward another corner, reach a ledge and pick a careful path around an enormous loose flake sitting on it. Easier ground up and left leads to a belay under the last steep corner.
Climb to a small sloping footledge, then right into a little corner; an awkward jug move gets you to the large corner above. Stay in it or exit right after a few moves to a belay ledge.
Quest up and right around the corner, then around the bulge to the top.

review.changed: Wrote 8 pitches and a 4-rappel table. Crux P5. Rappel station details thin, hedged; the uncertain count is noted. (Reviewer: rappel table removed; station order hedged.)
review.other_findings: Stored 8 pitches, 5.12+ agree. P5 can jam the rope; carry self-rescue gear.

pitch_detail.notes: The route starts in a large corner just to the right of the tower, with a piton roughly 20 ft above the ground. Climb to the pin, then trend slightly left toward some overhangs and belay in a crack.
Climb the crack briefly, then cross left around the arete and go up to a ledge under the white corner. Alternatively go further up and left to a ledge and belay in a 4 inch crack.

Up the corner to the ledge under the giant white corner; back-clean to limit rope drag. Go left on a ledge round the corner to a left-facing 4 inch crack, follow it up and back right, then toward an obvious 2-3 inch splitter all the way to a ledge belay.
Dirty, mossy right-facing corner to a ledge under the obvious left-facing corner.

Start in the splitter left of the corner to dodge the bushy start. Once past a solid #4 placement, cross right on incut crimps to the finger crack in the corner. A bulge with a hand crack comes next, then go right to the arete and up to a sloping stance under the crux corner.

A finger crack in a corner passes an awkward overhang, followed by stemming, face holds and a crumbly crack to a small roof where the stone turns to clean white granite. Rest and place solid gear, then a bouldery crux crosses the overhanging 0.3-0.5 crack. Loose blocks lie to the left after the difficulties. Move right on crimps around the corner to a chimney or crack, and belay below the overhanging blocks at the top of the tower.
Descend a little to the right and round the corner to avoid the loose overhanging blocks, then climb back up to a grungy corner and wet, mossy chimneys leading to the summit. An unpleasant finish.

review.changed: Wrote 7 pitches. Crux P6. No rappel table: one rappel off the back of the tower (about 100 ft) is described, not a station list.
review.other_findings: Stored 5.12a R; pitch 6 stated 5.12-. Descent: one rappel (about 30 m) off the northwest side from a fixed anchor (2024), or leave gear.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin to the left of the big dihedral, using thin cracks in a shallow corner. Follow the cracks and move right onto a small ledge for the belay.
Keep following the corner, passing a very old Star Drive bolt. A thin ramp leads to a hand crack, then move left around the arete to the face and belay beneath the roof.
Steep right-facing corner and cracks past a couple of scary blocks, then right onto the giant ledge. Very large loose flakes and blocks here must be avoided.
Ramp left to a ledge and a giant, wide right-facing corner.
Climb the broad corner and chimney, then left around the arete toward the wide crack, belaying at the tree. The upper part of the pitch overlaps an easier route.
Ramp toward the obvious overhang in the centre of the tower; belay on a ledge below it.
An overhanging hand-and-fist crack, then a steep finger crack on the right, then easy ground to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote 7 pitches. Crux P2 (top grade). Descent is a 4th-class scramble west; no rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin on the neighbouring route and climb through its crack crux, then move right under a small roof, where microcams give protection. Better placements appear at the end of that traverse, ahead of a 5.11 mantel. Easy terrain leads to an anchor.

Small cams and nuts protect the start above the anchor; a good fixed nut sits at a stance where placing gear is fiddly. Higher, bolts protect face climbing on granite edges up to the left side of a ledge, then move right to a two-bolt anchor.

The key pitch: fragile rock protected by bolts and one thin hands cam to a ledge with a horn, then committing moves on crisp granite edges above a shallow roof to the final bolt from good holds. Two paths on moderate ground lead to the top.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches without grades or lengths (none stated). No rappel table: single 70 m rope descent only.
review.other_findings: Stored 5.12b; text gives only a 5.11 mantel on P1.

pitch_detail.notes: A short pitch with one bolt to the first anchors; falling is a bad idea.
Five bolts plus gear. Sling a flake and keep thin hand-size gear for higher up. Staying on line gives the best rock.
Start right of the anchors and follow the easiest path, protected entirely by gear.

A slab with tiny holds and big exposure, with roughly seven bolts. Angle up and right around the green arete, then follow the bolts up the slab, keeping left close to the arete. Microcams supplement the bolts.

review.changed: Wrote approach pitch and P1-P3 with stated numbers. Crux P3. No rappel table: anchors exist at each station but station lengths are pitch lengths only, no ordered list.
review.other_findings: Stored 5.11 vs. P3 5.11(-). Rappel or walk off; pitches have bolted rappel anchors.

pitch_detail.notes: Move fast to a stance beneath the large rock bulge, or headwall, and get your partners out of the rockfall zone. Another option is to belay above the steep part, roughly 210 ft up.
The headwall goes most easily on the right; above it, more than 50 ft of rambling, sun-softened ice remains.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches with no grades or lengths (210 ft is hedged). No rappel table: rappels are described only in general terms (two double-rope rappels, optional third).
review.other_findings: Stored grade WI4 Steep Snow; spring climb with rockfall and avalanche exposure.

skip_reasons.co_south_rock_creek_buttress_feel_the_ra: No per-pitch text: only 'follow the topo line' and a single note about pitch 2.
